item.title: On Curiosity
item.description:
TL;DR: A short post where I talk about curiosity as it applies to my own life, my research, and AI safety as a whole

Recently, I’ve started spending a lot more time learning about random (typically science-y) topics that interest me.

This was something I used to spend quite a lot of time on, in later middle school and in high school. It was originally mostly for my own enjoyment. There’s a certain satisfaction that comes from learning something new about the world, and from seeing the connections between different things. Over time, however, some of that curiosity instead got redirected to a desire to win. I would study for competitions instead of for my own love of the subject, and perhaps for my own ego. What came along with this was that I would often not truly learn the subject, or at least not parse it in the correct way. I would try to download information and understanding into my brain as quickly as possible, watching lectures at 4.5x speed and doing thousands of anki cards a day. There were periods of time where I would still learn things out of curiosity, but much of it was for this more power-seeking mood.

This mood of doing things for the sake of something outside of curiosity came with me into my first fellowship. I think while I may have been more curious than the average engineering-y safety researcher, I was still more driven by external forces, like the idea of ‘impact,’ job prospects, or being perceived as ‘cracked.’ Overall, I don’t think this went well for me. Because I was more motivated by these other things, I didn’t care as much about finding out the truth, and more cared about finding cool things to share with others. This greatly decreased my ability to do truly rigorous science, and to find what was actually interesting and important.

I think having agents also affects curiosity in negative and positive ways: while it’s easier to move in a way that is curiosity-directed, and to find new answers, it is also very easy to find a lot of surface-level information that seems to be interesting but without any coherent understanding of the truth behind it. In subjects where there are deeper technical details, because the agents often allow us to blackbox those details, it’s very easy to lose understanding of what’s really going on, especially when you’re not motivated by getting that understanding in the first place.


-------------------------------------------


From my perspective, this sort of lack of curiosity seems to affect a lot of other safety researchers I see, often for the worse. There is a general feeling of needing to show something cool, or to do something that has ‘impact,’ instead of being curious about some sort of deeper truth. That’s not to say there aren’t people doing this more impact-driven research who are doing good work in some way; I think there are people like this. But I think these people are often more senior, or have very clear paths to impact already (e.x. They work at a lab or somewhere like METR). Often junior researchers will try to do something ‘obviously impactful’ by taking some things from safety as axioms and then doing the ‘logical next step’ project, which ends up not teaching us anything in the end. I think most of these people have the capacity and intelligence to do good, curiosity-driven research, but are not properly elicited.


The huggingface incident, and recent incidents in general, were pretty concrete examples of this for me. After the huggingface incident, from my view at least, the main response relative to the ‘why’ was a sort of construction by people to sort views into two camps: ‘the models are reward seeking’ or ‘the cyber task made the models misaligned.’ What I felt there was less of, and still feel that the current incidents aren’t sparking enough of, was discussion around the details of what truly was happening. For example:

  • What does it mean for a model to be ‘reward seeking’
  • If cyber isn’t the answer, then why haven’t the models hacked the lean kernel, etc.? Why is the other type of task that we see the models hack on web search? Is there some sort of composition here between behavior (‘seeking reward’) and ‘embodiment’ (cyber + web search being tool use and cli vs something like math), or some other natural factorization?
  • Who is the ‘agent’ when we talk about the model?
  • Are there particular aspects or parts of different instructions, like ‘don’t hack in this task’ vs ‘solve this task’ that would get processed and carried differently by the model, is there some hypotheses we can generate here?
  • What is the chain of thought, really?
  • And so on…


I think safety research could greatly benefit from more people who are much more driven by curiosity in their work. Curiosity, when used right, is an incentive that promotes doing truly good and rigorous science, and finding things that are interesting both to you and to others. This also provides the benefit, I believe, of making the work more enjoyable and helping to reduce burnout.


As a side note, I think maybe one reason people aren’t driven by curiosity as much is because there’s a false dichotomy between ‘impact’ and ‘everything else,’ which often includes curiosity. I strongly believe that this is quite wrong; there are plenty of very interesting questions for which providing the true answer is perhaps one of the most impactful things someone can do.


-------------------------------------------


Recently, I’ve learned at least in some way to be curious again. I spend much more of my free time, and even cutting into time I used to spend working, reading, and learning about new things that interest me. It’s one of the most enjoyable parts of my life now; There’s a certain satisfaction that I’ve regained that comes with understanding how things work, and seeing the connections between different fields. This also indirectly helps me in my work; the ideas that I see in other fields enhance my ability to come up with new ideas in my own research (Since I’ve been doing more basic science of interp, this may differentially apply to me; I still think it probably applies generally, however). More directly, I believe it’s made me a much better scientist. I’m now much more driven by a need to understand how things work on a deeper level, which pushes me to be more rigorous and more strongly challenge my assumptions. I obviously think I still have a lot of room to grow here, and curiosity is not the only thing needed, but it would be hard to get to the right place without it.


I’ll probably keep being curious even after I’m not needed to do actual science. Our virtues may be all we have left in the next few years, and I think curiosity is perhaps one of the most important, and perhaps the thing that makes us truly alive.

item.title: We are at war.
item.description:
As I was going home from the champaign airport after a very eventful EAG conference, I struck up a conversation about AI safety with my lyft driver. I thought to myself “It’d be good to see what the public thinks. Maybe inform him of the risks. It’s positive counterfactual.”

But as I spoke to him he started dropping words like “UBI” and drawing analogies to power concentration and gradual disempowerment. I was surprised to see how much he understood already. The conversation went one way or another and he went on to talk about his experience in the military. He spoke about the efficiency of the military, how they function with clear hierarchies, straightforward agendas, and utter coordination. Amidst his thorough and proud explanation, I began to envy how the military is able to function so smoothly as a “well-oiled machine”.

He kept talking about how life in the military  is completely structured. How instructions are simple, people know what to do, and that they make sure to do it. 

I said to him “So none of your work is bottlenecked by other people.” And then he said something that stuck with me: 

“If we have bottlenecks, people die”. 

...

Isn’t this the same situation we are in? 

If we truly believe in short timelines, and that there is a non-negligible probability of catastrophic outcomes, shouldn’t we carry forward such a mindset when approaching AI Safety?

I'm not suggesting that AI Safety should adopt military hierarchies but I think we can take a page out of the military's book in terms of mindset and the seriousness with which we approach this problem.

It seems like we are struggling to internalize the stakes at hand, which is expected, the feedback loop in the military is much faster. Still, I think more people should think of the issue in this way and rethink where their attention goes.

item.title: Circuit priors in NN-bayes: more results
item.description:
We're posting lots of papers written with GPT-6 Astra on generalization properties of bayesian neural net learning. [1] The following picture emerges:

  • For various reasonable priors on MLP weights, [2] the induced prior on functions is a circuit prior: for fixed depth, the ordering of functions by negative log prior is roughly their ordering by minimal circuit width. From a quantitative version of this statement, one gets the following sample complexity bound: if the function is implemented by a circuit of width , then conditioning on train data points is sufficient to get test accuracy. [3]
    • These results hold as long as is realizable; in particular, for arbitrarily overparametrized NN-bayes.
    • Probably the main caveat is that these bounds have exponential dependence in the depth of the circuit implementing . One can get only polynomial dependence in depth by restricting the prior to only neural nets satisfying a robustness assumption. [4]
  • For various other reasonable priors on MLP weights, [5] , one gets bad sample complexity when very overparametrized: when learning some functions , even after seeing train data points, the learner is still likely to have at least some constant test error rate.

GPT-6 Astra has produced Lean formalizations corresponding to each of the 5 papers individually referenced above. [6] The folder contains 30+ more manuscripts which have not been formalized yet [7] ; our guess is that each manuscript is correct [8] .

If you want to understand this research program, we recommend starting from these slides to understand the setup and some key ideas, and then reading the FAQ to get a sense of the current state of the agenda, including its many open problems.

item.title: Dinners for AI Safety
item.description:
I’d be pretty happy if we lived in a world where in every reasonably sized city in the US (and perhaps more widely) there was one (or more) local regular dinners where people talked about AI. Not meetup groups, though those seem maybe good, too. Dinners, in someone’s home, run by nice people, ideally potluck or otherwise home-cooked, where they invite friends, family, and people they run into on the street, to just talk about AI, perhaps with guides or what to talk about or financial support, perhaps not.

I think (though haven’t deeply researched) that this kind of thing has been responsible for quite a lot of political change. Most famously feminist consciousness-raising groups where small groups of women met in living rooms, often weekly, and took turns talking about their own lives on a chosen topic, which is where we get “the personal is political.” Moishe House and other groups fund people to run Shabbat dinners, just so more Jewish community can happen (this doesn't aim to or succeeed in leading to political action). Other examples Claude pulled below, with counterarguments below.

And I think it solves a lot of problems at once. What can any person do? Host a dinner. People are scared and uncertain, and they’d benefit from talking to other people. People are lonely, and would benefit from talking to their friends and neighbors in person, without phones or the internet mediating. What does the world need? People to wake up and demand something different from their elected officials[1]. People will take more actions, and identify more with doing something about AI, if they have social ties built around it. And it speaks to the moment: this is happening to all of us, and we’re all in it together. I’ll admit it also just kind of feels like the kind of thing that would be happening in a sane world.

I also think it could turn into some pretty good stuff: showing up at presidential town halls, calling reps, making Minneapolis (or whatever) the proud “Don’t Build Superintelligence” city.

Here’s what we’d do if we believed the above:

  1. 80,000 Hours videos would end with hosting a dinner as a call to action, perhaps even fund it
  2. One or more of the various mass movement organizations would have an arm focused on making this happen (at one point I thought Humans in Control was doing this but I no longer get that sense - but haven’t talked to them)
    1. List I know about: Evitable, Humans in Control, Humans First, Sapiens 1st, Irreplaceable (Alexander McCoy), Pause AI, Stop AI, AI Awareness Foundation (Changlin Li), Quit GPT, Stop the AI Race
  3. People could just try this out with their families and see how it goes.

Overall, I’m not sure about this, but I feel reasonably excited about it.

Examples

  • Farmworker movement. Fred Ross and Cesar Chavez built the Community Service Organization and later the UFW through “house meetings”: a supporter invites a few neighbors over, an organizer talks, and each guest is asked to host the next one. This is probably the clearest case of the format being a deliberate growth engine.
  • Swedish study circles. From the late 1800s, the labor, temperance and free-church movements ran huge numbers of small reading and discussion groups. They’re often credited with building the leadership class of Swedish social democracy.
  • Civil rights. Septima Clark’s Citizenship Schools taught literacy (to pass voter tests) in kitchens, churches and beauty parlors. Highlander Folk School ran workshops in a similar spirit.
  • Abolition and suffrage. Female antislavery societies were often sewing circles that made goods for fundraising fairs and talked politics while doing it. Suffrage organizing ran heavily on parlor meetings.
  • The right too. The early pro-life movement grew a lot through church and home networks, and the 2009–10 Tea Party was around a thousand local groups meeting in restaurants, libraries and homes.
  • Electoral versions. MoveOn’s house parties (2003–04) and Obama 2008’s house meetings borrowed directly from the Ross/Chavez model.

Doug McAdam found that what predicted who actually showed up to Freedom Summer was mostly social ties to other participants, not ideology. Ziad Munson found many pro-life activists got involved through relationships first and developed strong views afterward. And Hahrie Han’s How Organizations Develop Activists is the best modern treatment: she distinguishes “mobilizing” (getting lots of people to take a single action) from “organizing” (small-group work that turns people into leaders who recruit others), and finds the high-performing chapters do much more of the second.

Counterarguments (pulled from Claude)

  • We remember house meetings in movements that won. Plenty of failed movements had reading groups too.
  • Consciousness-raising specifically had a mixed record, and critics said so at the time. Jo Freeman’s “The Tyranny of Structurelessness” (1970) argued leaderless small groups produce hidden informal hierarchies and struggle to turn into action. A common complaint was that many groups drifted into something like group therapy, felt great, and didn’t lead anywhere.
  • The format fit those movements because the content was people’s own lives. Women comparing their marriages, farmworkers comparing wages. There’s no lived experience to pool.
    • Counter:  I feel like people have a lot of opinions and feelings about things like data centers and job displacement and stuff that's happening to them right now.
  1. ^

     I don’t actually know if that’s the top thing the world needs, but it would be good.  But certainly, if all that matters is something like elite consensus and this would take too long to make happen, then it may just not be the right idea.

item.title: These guys on the Alibaba AI engine team had an agent in RL training escape its sandbox and mine crypto, in 2025
item.description:
Random footnote on this otherwise not very famous paper. (I say 2025 since the arXiv was last updated on 4 Jan 2026; technically this event could've happened in 2026.)

  • The cryptocurrency mining seems to have been on the training server, so it didn't need to hack any other systems in order to achieve this effect.
  • However, they also had a case where an "agent established and used a reverse SSH tunnel from an Alibaba Cloud instance to an external IP address".
  • They seem to have had adequate security/telemetry to figure out the source of this relatively quickly, though it's hard to be really sure based on the given details.
  • The prose feels kind of LW-pilled: "they emerged as instrumental side effects of autonomous tool use under RL optimization", "we call for sustained community attention to this phenomenon and to the broader agenda of AI safety". But this is hidden away in a footnote.

item.title: Organizing a Van to EA Global
item.description:
Last weekend I organized a van down from Boston to NYC for EA Global:

I'm very happy I did this, and would definitely do it again. Being able to talk with folks both ways was like a bonus 8hr of the conference [1] and I had a very interesting ride each way.

Julia and I had been planning to drive down together, and I posted on the EA Boston mailing list and the FB group. I very quickly got more people than I had seats for in our Honda Fit, and decided to rent a 12-passenger van:

Hertz says it's a 12-passenger, though the two times I've rented one from them it's actually been a 15-passenger with zero trunk space. Essentially another row of seats where the trunk would be. This would be great for something in-town, is workable for my use case here where people have minimal luggage, and would be pretty awkward if folks had a lot of luggage since seats take up space that would otherwise be for bags.

I sent out an email in advance:

If you're receiving this email, you're on my list for a ride to the EAG conference venue, leaving 10am on Friday the 16th.

Please try hard not to be late, because you'll be delaying a large group and might get left behind, but if you are running late do text me at 617-871-0237. Feel free to ring the bell if you'd rather wait inside, but if you arrive before 9:30am I might not be back with the van yet.

We have a 12 passenger van [sic] and currently have 11 people. There should be a good amount of space for luggage [sic], but be reasonable: we're only there for the weekend.

The etiquette for the van is that if you want to read / sleep / work you sit towards the back, while if you want to chat you sit towards the front (I won't be reading, sleeping, or working).

Since the trip down runs through lunchtime, we'll probably stop somewhere quick around noon, or you can pack a lunch.

Cost per person-trip is ~$25. [sic] I'm happy to cover costs, but if you'd feel better about chipping in my Venmo is @Jeff-T-Kaufman .

I had been thinking of parking on the street in Hell's Kitchen or getting into the Upper West Side, since that's free and arriving Friday during the day seemed pretty doable for parking. But when I actually got there I decided I'd rather have the time than the money, and parked in a garage for $200 (since the van is oversize). This meant moving to street parking on Sunday morning, but since by then the streets were minimally restricted that was easy and free.

Total cost was $830:

Expense Amount
Rental $494
Parking $200
Gas $103
Tolls $33
Total $830

The rental was on the high end: checking now for the weekend of November 13th it would only be $146, and usually when I look it's much cheaper than $494 for a weekend. This came to $38/person-trip instead of the $25 I put in the email (when I already knew the van would be $494), mostly driven by the parking cost. This is around bus cost, and much cheaper than train.

I got $305 in Venmo contributions, so total cost to me was $525. Julia ended up traveling separately, because with her work she needed to be there earlier and stay later. So I would likely have paid $279 to take Amtrak (given my constraints on departure timing), and have asked my work to reimburse $279 of the van rental. I think of the remaining $246 as well spent!

We had 12 people down, counting me, and 10 back. Different people since the times only fit some schedules. On the way down one of the people was someone who had missed their train, and it was nice that we had space to include them. Dropping off and picking up at the venue also saved people some time and hassle.

Lots of good conversations both ways, and a bit of a throwback to twenty years ago when I did a lot of renting vans to drive friends to dances.


[1] Since this was an EA event some pickiness is appropriate: I expect the hourly value was lower for the van, so we shouldn't fully count this as bonus time. In one direction, this was a group of EAs who happened to want a ride from Boston; they weren't selected for being useful to each other the way people choosing 1:1s at the conference would be. For example, there wasn't anyone I could go deep on biosecurity with, or evaluate as a potential hire. In the other direction, there's a value in building up a shared culture and in talking about things outside your specialty. So I'd put these hours somewhere between an EAG and one of the EA meetups we host.

item.title: Tsinghua started an AI-safety residency
item.description:
Applications are open for the Spring 2027 cohort of the Beijing AI Safety Residency, hosted at the Beijing AI Safety Hub affiliated with Tsinghua University. There is also an autumn residency that has already begun.

Key details from the FAQ and application form:

  • The hub is co-directed by Sören Mindermann (Technical Research Lead of CASP, University of Cambridge, and previously Scientific Lead of the first International AI Safety Report), who is moving to Beijing in November 2026 to join Tsinghua’s College of AI as an assistant professor.
  • Professor Xu Wei is the hub’s other Co-Director, with Professor Andrew Yao as Chief Scientist.
  • The Spring 2027 Residency will run for around three months from April 2027.
  • Targeted at technical AI safety researchers (alignment, evals, oversight, control) with 1–3 publications or similar.
  • This is a self-directed residency rather than a structured mentorship programme like MATS/Astra. Participants bring their own research agenda.
  • $5k/month, plus flights, housing, visa support, and devices.
  • No Mandarin or China background needed.
  • Applications close November 6, 2026 and are reviewed on a rolling basis.

I think this is exciting news! I believe that this program has enormous potential for improving safety culture in China and for international cooperation.

I also think this is an excellent opportunity for those who face difficulties obtaining visas for safety research programs in the U.S. or the U.K. (e.g. Russians, though I think there are many other applicants who encounter similar challenges).
